nameStory: The "wharf louse" gets its name from its favorite hangout spots - the wooden pilings, concrete walls, and rocky surfaces around harbors and wharves. Like its terrestrial cousin the wood louse (or "roly-poly"), it's called a "louse" because of its flattened, segmented body, though it's not actually related to true lice at all.
description: The wharf louse is a small, flattened crustacean that looks like a cross between a pill bug and a tiny armored tank. These gray to brownish creatures are usually about half an inch to an inch long, with seven pairs of legs and long antennae that they wave around constantly. Unlike the pill bugs you might find in your garden, wharf lice can't roll into a ball and prefer to scurry quickly across wet surfaces. They're actually more closely related to shrimp and crabs than to insects, even though they live on land.

idTips.label: Body shape and movement
idTips.description: Flattened, oval body that moves with a distinctive quick, scuttling motion across surfaces - they can't roll into a ball like pill bugs

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of long antennae that are constantly moving and twitching - the outer pair is noticeably longer than the body

idTips.label: Color and texture
idTips.description: Mottled gray to brownish coloration with a slightly rough, segmented texture that feels firm but not hard when gently touched

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Seven pairs of walking legs visible along the sides - count them if you can get a still view

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: About the size of your thumbnail, typically half an inch to an inch long

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Extremely quick to dart into cracks and crevices when disturbed, preferring to stay near the waterline on wet surfaces

habitat: In New England, look for wharf lice on harbor walls, pier pilings, rocky shorelines, and breakwaters right around the high tide line. They prefer spots that stay damp from sea spray but aren't submerged, often hiding in cracks between rocks or under seaweed during the day. You'll have the best luck finding them on protected coastlines rather than exposed, wave-battered shores.

seasonality.spring: Become more active as temperatures warm, often seen scuttling across wet pier surfaces during low tide periods.
seasonality.summer: Most active and easiest to spot during warm evenings, when they venture out to feed on decaying seaweed and organic matter.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may be slower moving in cooler weather, often found clustered together under driftwood or in rock crevices.
seasonality.winter: Much less active and harder to find, hiding deep in protected cracks and crevices where they can avoid freezing.

funFact: Despite living on land and breathing air, wharf lice still need to keep their gills moist to survive - they're essentially marine animals that have learned to live out of water, but never strayed far from the sea!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with pill bugs (roly-polies) found in gardens, but wharf lice are exclusively coastal, can't roll into balls, and have much longer antennae. Remember: "Wharf lice wave long antennae, pill bugs make perfect balls."
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name "louse" fool you - these aren't parasites and won't bother you at all. They're actually beneficial cleanup crew members, munching on rotting seaweed and organic debris along the shoreline. The "exotic" in their scientific name refers to their wide global distribution, not that they're particularly foreign to New England waters.
compareHints: The wharf louse is extremely similar to its close relative, the common sea slater, and telling them apart requires close examination of small anatomical features that are difficult to see in the field. Both species live in nearly identical coastal habitats and have similar gray coloring and quick movements. For practical field identification purposes, any sea slater you find scuttling around New England's rocky shores or harbor structures is most likely one of these two species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Common Sea Slater is distinguished from its relative the Wharf Louse by its larger size and preference for natural rocky shores rather than harbors and docks.
